problem:
A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(\sqrt{2}t,\sqrt{2}t),$ where $t$ is a positive real number. Find the polar coordinates of $P$ expressed in terms of $t.$ Give the polar angle in radians and do not round the answer.

Expressed in terms of $t,$ the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2}t)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the point $P$ lies in the first quadrant, we can determine $\theta $ by taking the arctangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}t}{\sqrt{2}t}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(2t,\frac{\pi }{4}).$
